stances.claim: Sen. Robin Padilla, the 2022 senatorial topnotcher, personally signed under oath and filed a petition on Aug 5 -- 'by his lonesome -- without being represented or assisted by lawyers' -- asking the SC for a binding opinion on what 'a vote of three-fourths of all its Members' means under Article XVII Section 1, the question on which his Senate committee's invited legal experts could not agree.

The substantive controversy: joint-voting view sums senators and congressmen and extracts 3/4 from the total; separate-voting view treats the two Houses independently. 'Most senators insist on separate voting; otherwise, they would drown in the sea of the much more numerous representatives, who, understandably, want joint voting.'
Padilla concedes he is asking for 'declaratory relief' (Rule 63 Section 1) which 'should be filed in the Regional Trial Courts (RTCs)' but pleads exception due to 'transcendental importance.'

CJ admires Padilla's 'patriotic intentions' but identifies three difficult remedial-law problems: (1) declaratory-relief jurisdiction is initially in RTCs, SC only on appeal -- though SC has granted 'transcendental importance' exceptions; (2) the petition includes no opposing party -- 'our judicial system is essentially adversarial in nature' with justices/judges as 'passive participants'; (3) the petition pleads for an 'advisory opinion' which our Constitution does not allow (unlike the ICJ).

CJ's procedural recommendation: the Court should NOT simply dismiss -- because Padilla furnished copies to OSG, Senate President, and Speaker -- but should let them intervene voluntarily or be directed to file comments 'to comply with the constitutional edicts of due process,' and then 'promulgate a full decision and thereby avoid issuing an advisory opinion.'

one_paragraph_summary: Sen. Robinhood C. Padilla, the 2022 senatorial topnotcher, personally signed under oath and filed on August 5 a petition -- 'by his lonesome -- without being represented or assisted by lawyers' -- asking the Supreme Court for a binding opinion on how Congress should vote in revising or amending the Constitution. He quoted Article XVII: Section 1 (amendments/revisions proposed by Congress 'upon a vote of three-fourths of all its Members') and Section 3 ('two-thirds of all its Members' to call a concon; 'majority vote' to submit concon-calling to the electorate). As chair of the Senate committee on constitutional amendment and revision of codes, the 54-year-old 'champion of federalism' has called public hearings, but invited legal experts could not agree on the meaning of 'vote of three-fourths.' One camp argues joint voting (sum senators + congressmen, extract 3/4); another argues separate voting (as in ordinary legislation). 'Most senators insist on separate voting; otherwise, they would drown in the sea of the much more numerous representatives, who, understandably, want joint voting.' Padilla frames the irreconcilable differences as 'actual controversy' or 'gloomy atmosphere' and pleads transcendental national interest. He concedes he is asking for 'declaratory relief' (Rule 63 Section 1) which 'should be filed in the Regional Trial Courts (RTCs)' but asks for an exception due to 'transcendental importance.' CJ deeply admires Padilla's patriotic intentions but identifies -- IMHO -- three difficult remedial-law problems. FIRST, declaratory-relief jurisdiction is initially vested in RTCs with SC review only on appeal; though SC has granted exceptions for 'transcendental importance' in rare cases, it could dismiss the petition on short shrift. SECOND, the petition includes no opposing party with adverse interest, but 'our judicial system is essentially adversarial in nature. Justices and judges are passive participants in conducting trials in the lower courts and in reviewing the records when they pass upon appeals.' THIRD -- flowing from the second -- Padilla is asking for an 'advisory opinion' which 'our Constitution does not allow the judiciary to promulgate' (unlike the International Court of Justice and some foreign tribunals). CJ recommends: the Court should NOT simply dismiss given the transcendental issue. Because Padilla already furnished copies to OSG, Senate President, and Speaker, the Court should let them intervene voluntarily or be directed to file comments -- to comply with 'the constitutional edicts of due process' -- and then 'promulgate a full decision and thereby avoid issuing an advisory opinion.' CJ closes: 'Should Padilla win this case on its merits despite its seemingly insurmountable procedural mountain peaks, he could be admitted to the Philippine Bar and become a full-fledged lawyer as an exception to the Rules of Court's requirement to pass a four-year basic law degree and the stringent bar exam.'
